# Natural Language Processing

## Learning Objectives
- Explain how text can be represented computationally.
- Build text-classification pipelines.
- Compare bag-of-words, TF-IDF, and embeddings.
- Explain the intuition behind transformers.
- Evaluate NLP models responsibly.

## Why This Matters
A large share of human knowledge is stored as text. NLP enables machine learning with documents, responses, reports, and other unstructured language data.

## Real-World Problem
Can open-ended student responses or health narratives be analyzed reliably without reducing nuanced language to misleading labels?

## Hands-On Practice
Build a reproducible text classifier and compare sparse and embedding-based representations.

## Common Mistakes
- Leakage from duplicated or related documents.
- Random splitting when time or source matters.
- Ignoring class and language imbalance.
- Treating model-generated labels as ground truth.

## Knowledge Check
1. What does TF-IDF represent?
2. How are contextual embeddings different from bag-of-words features?
3. What problem does attention address?
4. Why can random splitting inflate NLP performance?

## Real-World Case Study
### Analyzing Educational Text
Develop a research-safe NLP workflow using a publicly available text corpus.

## Professor's Challenge
An automated text classifier agrees with human coders 85% of the time. Is that sufficient for research use?

## Research Extension
Compare human and machine coding, domain transfer, or robustness across populations.

## Reproducibility Check
Version corpora, document preprocessing, preserve split logic, and record model/checkpoint identifiers.

## Key Takeaways
- Text representation strongly shapes NLP performance.
- Transformers provide contextual representations but introduce new reproducibility challenges.
- Human validation remains important.
